cards.waite_pd_excerpt: Waite reads the card as folly, extravagance and intoxication with life, a free spirit setting out without counting the cost. Reversed it points to negligence, carelessness and a choice made without thought.

For Waite the Magician means skill, diplomacy and self-confidence, the will directed toward a goal; it can also hint at subtlety or sickness. Reversed it becomes the physician, the mountebank, mental unease and disgrace.

Waite calls her secrets, mystery and the future still unrevealed, the silent and wise woman who interests the querent. Reversed she signals passion, moral or physical ardour, conceit and shallow knowledge.

Waite associates the Empress with fruitfulness, initiative, action, long days and the unknown made clear; she is also doubt and difficulty resolved. Reversed she suggests light, truth and the unravelling of tangled matters, or public rejoicing, though some readers see vacillation.

In Waite the Emperor stands for stability, power, protection and realisation, a great person, aid, reason and conviction. Reversed he indicates benevolence, compassion and credit, but also confusion to enemies and obstruction.

Waite reads the Hierophant as marriage, alliance, captivity and servitude; by another account, mercy, goodness and inspiration, the person to whom the querent turns. Reversed it is society, good understanding, concord, over-kindness and weakness.

Waite gives the Lovers as attraction, love and beauty, trials overcome. Reversed it signals failure and foolish designs; another account reads it as marriage frustrated and contrarieties of every kind.
For Waite the Chariot means succour, providence, war, triumph, presumption and vengeance, trouble in some readings. Reversed it points to riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation and defeat.
Waite assigns Strength to power, energy, action and courage, magnanimity and complete success with honours. Reversed it shows despotism, abuse of power, weakness, discord and sometimes disgrace.
Waite reads the Hermit as prudence and circumspection, but also treason, dissimulation, roguery and corruption. Reversed it means concealment, disguise, policy, fear and unreasoned caution.
Waite calls the Wheel destiny, fortune, success, elevation, luck and felicity. Reversed it means increase, abundance and superfluity.

Waite gives Justice as equity, rightness, probity and executive power, triumph of the deserving side in law. Reversed it is law in all its departments, legal complications, bigotry, bias and excessive severity.
Waite describes the Hanged Man as wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice, intuition, divination and prophecy. Reversed it stands for selfishness, the crowd and the body politic.

Waite reads Death as end, mortality, destruction and corruption; for a man the loss of a benefactor, for a woman many contrarieties, for a maid failure of marriage projects. Reversed it means inertia, sleep, lethargy, petrifaction, somnambulism and hope destroyed.

For Waite Temperance signifies economy, moderation, frugality, management and accommodation. Reversed it concerns churches, religions, sects and the priesthood, sometimes a querent set to marry a priest; also disunion, unfortunate combinations and competing interests.

Waite assigns the Devil to ravage, violence, vehemence, extraordinary efforts, force and fatality, that which is predestined but not for this reason evil. Reversed it is evil fatality, weakness, pettiness and blindness.

Waite reads the Tower as misery, distress, indigence, adversity, calamity, disgrace, deception and ruin; it is a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe. Reversed it is the same in a lesser degree, with oppression, imprisonment and tyranny.
Waite calls the Star loss, theft, privation and abandonment, yet another reading is hope and bright prospects. Reversed it means arrogance, haughtiness and impotence.

For Waite the Moon means hidden enemies, danger, calumny, darkness, terror, deception, occult forces and error. Reversed it signals instability, inconstancy, silence and lesser degrees of deception and error.
Waite assigns the Sun to material happiness, fortunate marriage and contentment. Reversed it carries the same meanings in a lesser sense.

Waite reads Judgement as change of position, renewal and outcome; another account speaks of a lawsuit that is lost. Reversed it is weakness, pusillanimity, simplicity, deliberation, decision and sentence.
Waite gives the World as assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight and change of place. Reversed it is inertia, fixity, stagnation and permanence.

Waite reads the Ace of Wands as creation, invention, enterprise and the powers that result in these, a beginning, birth, family or origin, and the source of enterprises. Reversed it is fall, decadence, ruin, perdition and a clouded joy.

Waite sees in the Two of Wands riches, fortune and magnificence, yet also the sadness of one who holds the world and finds it empty; physical suffering, disease, chagrin and sadness are listed. Reversed it means surprise, wonder, enchantment, emotion, trouble and fear.

Waite calls the Three of Wands established strength, enterprise, effort, trade, commerce and discovery; the merchant watches his ships come in. Reversed it is the end of troubles, suspension or cessation of adversity, toil and disappointment.

For Waite the Four of Wands means country life, a haven of refuge, a harvest home, repose, concord, harmony, prosperity, peace and the perfected work of these. Reversed it reads as prosperity, increase, felicity, beauty and embellishment unchanged.

Waite reads the Five of Wands as imitation, sham fight, the strenuous competition and struggle of the search after riches and fortune, also gold, gain and opulence. Reversed it means litigation, disputes, trickery and contradiction.

Waite gives the Six of Wands as a victor triumphing, great news, expectation crowned with its own desire, the crown of hope. Reversed it is apprehension, fear of a victorious enemy, treachery, disloyalty and indefinite delay.

Waite reads the Seven of Wands as valour, a card of success in discussion, business negotiation, barter and competition, the man holding a position of vantage. Reversed it means perplexity, embarrassments, anxiety and a caution against indecision.

For Waite the Eight of Wands means activity in undertakings, the path of such activity, swiftness as of an express messenger, great haste, great hope, speed towards an assured end, and the arrows of love. Reversed it is the arrow of jealousy, internal dispute, stings of conscience and quarrels.

Waite reads the Nine of Wands as strength in opposition, the figure ready to meet attack; the card signifies delay, suspension and adjournment. Reversed it indicates obstacles, adversity and calamity.

Waite calls the Ten of Wands oppression, fortune, gain and success together with the weight they bring; if a lawsuit is pending there will be certain loss. Reversed it is contrarieties, difficulties, intrigues and their analogies.

Waite reads the Page of Wands as a dark young man, faithful, a lover, an envoy or postman; beside a man he bears favourable testimony, and a dangerous rival if followed by the Page of Cups. Reversed it is anecdotes, announcements, evil news, indecision and instability.
Waite describes the Knight of Wands as departure, absence, flight, emigration, a dark young man friendly, change of residence. Reversed it is rupture, division, interruption and discord.

For Waite the Queen of Wands is a dark woman, countrywoman, friendly, chaste, loving, honourable; near a man she signifies love of money or success in business. Reversed she is good, economical, obliging and serviceable, but may also signify opposition, jealousy, deceit and infidelity.

Waite reads the King of Wands as a dark man, friendly, countryman, generally married, honest and conscientious; the card signifies honesty and may mean news of an unexpected heritage. Reversed he is good but severe, austere yet tolerant.

Waite calls the Ace of Cups the house of the true heart, joy, content, abode, nourishment, abundance, fertility and holy table. Reversed it is the house of the false heart, mutation, instability and revolution.

For Waite the Two of Cups means love, passion, friendship, affinity, union, concord, sympathy and the interrelation of the sexes, together with the desire that is not in nature but by which nature is sanctified. He gives no reversed meaning; later tradition reads disharmony.

Waite reads the Three of Cups as the conclusion of any matter in plenty, perfection and merriment, happy issue, victory, fulfilment, solace and healing. Reversed it is expedition, dispatch, achievement and end, also excess in physical enjoyment.

Waite calls the Four of Cups weariness, disgust, aversion and imaginary vexations, as if the wine of the world had only brought satiety; another wine is offered yet brings no consolation. Reversed it is novelty, presage, new instruction and new relations.

Waite reads the Five of Cups as a card of loss, but something remains over; three have been taken yet two are left; a card of inheritance, patrimony and transmission, though not answering to expectations, and sometimes marriage with bitterness or frustration. Reversed it means news, alliances, affinity, consanguinity, ancestry, return and false projects.

For Waite the Six of Cups is a card of the past and of memories, looking back as on childhood, happiness, enjoyment coming from the past, things that have vanished; another reading gives new relations, new knowledge and a new environment. Reversed it is the future, renewal and that which will come to pass presently.

Waite reads the Seven of Cups as fairy favours, images of reflection, sentiment, imagination and things seen in the glass of contemplation, some attainment in these degrees but nothing permanent or substantial. Reversed it is desire, will, determination and project.

Waite gives the Eight of Cups as the decline of a matter, or that a matter thought important is really of slight consequence, either for good or evil; also giving joy, mildness, timidity, honour and modesty. Reversed it is great joy, happiness and feasting.

Waite calls the Nine of Cups concord, contentment and physical well-being, also victory, success and advantage, satisfaction for the querent. Reversed it is truth, loyalty and liberty, but also mistakes and imperfections.

For Waite the Ten of Cups means contentment and repose of the whole heart, the perfection of human love and friendship; if with several picture cards, a person taking charge of the querent’s interests; also the town or country of residence. Reversed it is repose of the false heart, indignation and violence.

Waite reads the Page of Cups as a fair young man impelled to render service, a studious youth, news, message, application, reflection and meditation, directed to business. Reversed he is taste, inclination, attachment, seduction, deception and artifice.

For Waite the Knight of Cups is arrival, approach, sometimes that of a messenger, advances, proposition, demeanour, invitation and incitement. Reversed he is trickery, artifice, subtlety, swindling, duplicity and fraud.

Waite calls the Queen of Cups good, fair woman, honest and devoted, who will do service to the querent; loving intelligence and hence the gift of vision, success, happiness, pleasure, wisdom and virtue. Reversed she is a distinguished woman but not to be trusted, perversity, vice, dishonour and depravity.

Waite reads the King of Cups as a fair man, man of business, law or divinity, responsible, disposed to oblige the querent; also equity, art and science, including those who profess science, law and art, creative intelligence. Reversed he is a dishonest, double-dealing man, roguery, exaction, injustice, vice, scandal and loss.

Waite reads the Ace of Swords as triumph, the excessive degree in everything, conquest and triumph of force; a card of great force in love as well as in hatred. Reversed it is the same results but disastrous, conception, childbirth, augmentation and multiplicity.

Waite gives the Two of Swords as conformity and the equipoise it suggests, courage, friendship, concord in a state of arms; another reading gives tenderness, affection and intimacy. Reversed it is imposture, falsehood, duplicity and disloyalty.

Waite reads the Three of Swords as removal, absence, delay, division, rupture, dispersion and all that the design signifies naturally, being too simple and obvious to need specific enumeration. Reversed it is mental alienation, error, loss, distraction, disorder and confusion.

For Waite the Four of Swords means vigilance, retreat, solitude, hermit’s repose, exile, tomb and coffin, the last being what the design suggests. Reversed it is wise administration, circumspection, economy, avarice, precaution and testament.
Waite reads the Five of Swords as degradation, destruction, revocation, infamy, dishonour and loss, with the variants and analogues of these. Reversed it is the same, also burial and obsequies.
For Waite the Six of Swords means journey by water, route, way, envoy, commissionary and expedient. Reversed it is declaration, confession, publicity; one account says it is a proposal of love.

Waite calls the Seven of Swords design, attempt, wish, hope, confidence, also quarrelling, a plan that may fail, and annoyance; the design is uncertain in its import. Reversed it is good advice, counsel, instruction, slander and babbling.

Waite reads the Eight of Swords as bad news, violent chagrin, crisis, censure, power in trammels, conflict, calumny and also sickness. Reversed it is disquiet, difficulty, opposition, accident, treachery, the unforeseen and fatality.
For Waite the Nine of Swords means death, failure, miscarriage, delay, deception, disappointment and despair. Reversed it is imprisonment, suspicion, doubt, reasonable fear and shame.

Waite reads the Ten of Swords as whatsoever is intimated by the design: pain, affliction, tears, sadness and desolation, though it is not especially a card of violent death. Reversed it is advantage, profit, success, favour, but none of these permanent; also power and authority.

Waite reads the Page of Swords as authority, overseeing, secret service, vigilance, spying, examination and the qualities thereto belonging. Reversed it is the more evil side of these qualities, what is unforeseen, an unprepared state, sickness is also intimated.

For Waite the Knight of Swords means skill, bravery, capacity, defence, address, enmity, wrath, war, destruction, opposition, resistance and ruin; there is therefore a sense in which the card signifies death, but it carries this meaning only in proximity to other cards of fatality. Reversed it is imprudence, incapacity and extravagance.

Waite calls the Queen of Swords widowhood, female sadness and embarrassment, absence, sterility, mourning, privation and separation. Reversed she is malice, bigotry, artifice, prudery, bale and deceit.

Waite reads the King of Swords as whatsoever arises out of the idea of judgment and all its connexions: power, command, authority, militant intelligence, law and offices of the crown. Reversed he is cruelty, perversity, barbarity, perfidy and evil intention.

Waite reads the Ace of Pentacles as perfect contentment, felicity, ecstasy, also speedy intelligence and gold. Reversed it is the evil side of wealth, bad intelligence, also great riches; in any case it shows prosperity and comfortable material conditions.

For Waite the Two of Pentacles means gaiety and recreation on one hand, and on the other news and messages in writing, obstacles, agitation, trouble and embroilment. Reversed it is enforced gaiety, simulated enjoyment, literal sense, handwriting, composition and letters of exchange.

Waite calls the Three of Pentacles the craftsman, skilled labour, usually shown as a card of nobility, aristocracy, renown and glory. Reversed it is mediocrity in work and otherwise, puerility, pettiness and weakness.
Waite reads the Four of Pentacles as the surety of possessions, cleaving to that which one has, gift, legacy and inheritance. Reversed it is suspense, delay and opposition.

For Waite the Five of Pentacles foretells material trouble above all, whether in the form of destitution or otherwise; for some it is a card of love and lovers, wife, husband, friend, mistress, also concordance and affinities. Reversed it is disorder, chaos, ruin, discord and profligacy.

Waite reads the Six of Pentacles as presents, gifts, gratification, another account says attention, vigilance, now is the accepted time and present prosperity. Reversed it is desire, cupidity, envy, jealousy and illusion.

Waite calls the Seven of Pentacles money, business, barter, but one reading gives altercation and quarrels, another innocence, ingenuity and purgation. Reversed it is cause for anxiety regarding money which it may be proposed to lend.

For Waite the Eight of Pentacles means work, employment, commission, craftsmanship, skill in craft and business, perhaps in the preparatory stage. Reversed it is voided ambition, vanity, cupidity, exaction and usury; it may also signify the possession of skill in the sense of the ingenious mind turned to cunning and intrigue.
Waite reads the Nine of Pentacles as prudence, safety, success, accomplishment, certitude and discernment. Reversed it is roguery, deception, voided project and bad faith.

Waite reads the Ten of Pentacles as gain, riches, family matters, archives, extraction and the abode of a family. Reversed it is chance, fatality, loss, robbery, games of hazard, sometimes gift, dowry and pension.

For Waite the Page of Pentacles means application, study, scholarship, reflection, another reading says news, messages and the bringer thereof, also rule and management. Reversed it is prodigality, dissipation, liberality, luxury and unfavourable news.

Waite reads the Knight of Pentacles as utility, serviceableness, interest, responsibility, rectitude, all on the normal and external plane. Reversed he is inertia, idleness, repose of that kind, stagnation, also placidity, discouragement and carelessness.
For Waite the Queen of Pentacles means opulence, generosity, magnificence, security and liberty. Reversed she is evil, suspicion, suspense, fear and mistrust.

Waite reads the King of Pentacles as valour, realising intelligence, business and normal intellectual aptitude, sometimes mathematical gifts and attainments of this kind, success in these paths. Reversed he is vice, weakness, ugliness, perversity, corruption and peril.
